content: Radiographic imaging, such as chest X-rays, should not be a mandatory requirement or a barrier to initiating tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment in people living with HIV (PLHIV). This is due to the additional resources required and the minimal improvement in negative predictive value. However, it is important to note that in PLHIV with low CD4 counts, active TB can still occur even if the chest radiograph appears normal. PLHIV who exhibit any of the four key symptoms of TB or have abnormal findings on chest radiography should be thoroughly evaluated for active TB and other potential diseases. The Xpert® MTB/RIF test is recommended as the initial diagnostic tool in such cases. Preventive treatment should not be withheld from asymptomatic individuals at risk of TB infection, even if latent TB infection (LTBI) testing or chest radiography is unavailable. For example, PLHIV who are household contacts of TB patients should still be considered for preventive treatment, with appropriate adaptations to the triage process. It is essential to ensure proper follow-up and evaluation for TB and other diseases in household contacts who present with abnormal chest radiographic findings or TB symptoms. These investigations should align with national guidelines and sound clinical practices. Contacts who are found not to have active TB should be assessed for eligibility for preventive treatment. A history of prior TB or TB preventive treatment should not be considered a contraindication for initiating preventive treatment in cases of exposure, provided reactivated disease has been excluded. Individuals with fibrotic radiological lesions may be at increased risk of disease progression and should be managed accordingly. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on TB prevention emphasize the importance of follow-up for active TB, even in patients who have completed preventive treatment. For children under 10 years of age, specific symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, weight loss, or growth curve flattening should prompt further evaluation. Asymptomatic infants under 1 year of age with HIV should only be treated for LTBI if they are household contacts of TB patients. Testing for LTBI using tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) can help identify PLHIV who would benefit most from preventive treatment. Chest radiography may also be used in PLHIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) before starting LTBI treatment. In children under 5 years of age, additional symptoms such as anorexia, failure to thrive, or decreased activity should be considered when determining if they are asymptomatic. For individuals with specific risk factors, such as silicosis, dialysis, anti-TNF agent treatment, or preparation for transplantation, national guidelines should be followed. Conditions like acute or chronic hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (if isoniazid is used), and heavy alcohol consumption should also be considered when planning treatment. Pregnancy or a history of TB are not contraindications for preventive treatment. Testing for LTBI increases the certainty that targeted individuals will benefit from treatment, but there is no gold standard test for diagnosing LTBI. Both TST and IGRA are indirect tests that require a competent immune response to identify TB infection. A positive result from either test does not reliably predict the risk of progression to active disease. The WHO guidelines recommend either TST or IGRA for LTBI testing, with both tests considered equivalent options. However, TST may require fewer resources and is more familiar to practitioners in resource-limited settings, though global shortages of TST reagents pose challenges. IGRA testing, while more costly and requiring laboratory infrastructure, has the advantage of not being affected by prior Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination. Neither TST nor IGRA should be used to diagnose active TB disease or as part of the diagnostic workup for adults suspected of having active TB. Preventive treatment options for LTBI include daily isoniazid for 6 or 9 months, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. In settings with high TB transmission, PLHIV with unknown or positive LTBI test results and no evidence of active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, or pregnancy. Shorter regimens containing rifamycins, such as daily rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months, have been shown to be as effective and safe as longer isoniazid monotherapy regimens. These shorter regimens are particularly advantageous in settings with limited resources. For multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), preventive treatment requires a different approach using fluoroquinolones or other second-line agents. The choice of regimen should consider factors such as age, drug susceptibility, risk of toxicity, availability, and patient preferences.
